identity.title: The Subterahertz Solar Cycle: Polar and Equatorial Radii Derived from SST and ALMA

paper_type_evidence.quote: In this work we determine the mean equatorial and mean polar radii of the Sun at 100, 212, 230, and 405 GHz using single-dish observations from the Solar Submillimeter-wave Telescope (SST) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).

question.value: Measure equatorial and polar subterahertz solar radii and investigate their relationship with the solar activity cycle.

evidence.quote: In this work we determine the mean equatorial and mean polar radii of the Sun at 100, 212, 230, and 405 GHz using single-dish observations from the Solar Submillimeter-wave Telescope (SST) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).
Moreover, we present an investigation about the relation between subterahertz radii time series and solar activity cycle proxies
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA #2011.0.00020.SV
The nominal spatial resolutions, HPBW, are ${58}^{\prime\prime}$ and ${25}^{\prime\prime}$ at 100 (Band 3) and 230 GHz (Band 6), respectively.

frequencies_and_spectral_setup.value: ALMA: 100 and 230 GHz; SST: 212 and 405 GHz

evidence.quote: daily solar observations of the Solar Submillimeter-wave Telescope (cite: kaufmann08) at 212, and 405 GHz, and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (cite: wootten09) at 100 and 230 GHz.
From four solar single-dish observation campaigns between 2015 and 2018, we use 196 fast-scan maps (125 at 100 and 71 at 230 GHz).

angular_resolution.value: ALMA nominal HPBW: 58 arcsec at 100 GHz and 25 arcsec at 230 GHz; SST nominal HPBW: 4 arcminutes at 212 GHz and 2 arcminutes at 405 GHz

evidence.quote: The nominal spatial resolutions, HPBW, are ${58}^{\prime\prime}$ and ${25}^{\prime\prime}$ at 100 (Band 3) and 230 GHz (Band 6), respectively.

evidence.quote: From four solar single-dish observation campaigns between 2015 and 2018, we use 196 fast-scan maps (125 at 100 and 71 at 230 GHz).

analysis_steps.goal: Orient maps and extract limb points

method.value: Rotate solar North upwards, correct coordinates for Earth's orbital eccentricity, and identify scan-derivative maxima and minima as solar limb coordinates.

evidence.quote: The first step is to extract the solar limb coordinates from each map which are defined as the maximum and minimum points of the numerical differentiation
All solar maps are rotated so that the position of the solar North points upwards, and the coordinates are corrected according to the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit

evidence.quote: With this radius determination filter, only points with a center–to–limb distance between ${815}^{\prime\prime}$ ($0.85 R_{\theta}$) and ${1100}^{\prime\prime}$ ($1.15 R_{\theta}$) are considered.

validation.value: Limb-point filtering intended to reject active-region, instrumental-error, and high-opacity contamination

analysis_steps.goal: Fit equatorial and polar radii for each map

method.value: Fit circles to latitude-selected limb coordinates; calculate radius as the average center-to-limb distance; apply the same method to SST and ALMA.

evidence.quote: The solar limb coordinates are fit by a circle and the radius is calculated as the average of the center-to-limb distances.
The same method is applied to both telescopes, so that a comparison between the 212 GHz radius of SST and the 230 GHz radius of ALMA could be made.

key_parameters.value: Equatorial: 30° N to 30° S; polar: above 60° N and below 60° S

key_parameters.value: Retain at least 35% of limb points, usually 6 out of 16; otherwise discard the map

referee_caveats_inferred: The statement that all four radii correlate more strongly with |B| than with F10.7 conflicts with Table 3: only the 212-GHz equatorial coefficient is larger in absolute value for |B|.
No correlation uncertainties, significance estimates, or correction for dependence introduced by smoothing are provided.
The iterative circle-fit stopping rule is ambiguous because the stated minimum retained fraction does not specify convergence.
Quoted radius uncertainties are not explicitly defined as scatter, errors on means, or combined systematic uncertainties.
The short ALMA series supports qualitative temporal comparisons but does not establish a complete solar-cycle relationship.
The limb-brightening explanation for the 100-GHz discrepancy remains a proposed mechanism rather than a measured time-dependent correction.
